claim: Ptpmt1 is encoded by nuclear DNA and is localized to the mitochondrion and anchored at the inner membrane.
source: Ptpmt1, encoded by nuclear DNA, is localized to the mitochondrion and anchored at the inner membrane (Pagliarini et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pagliarini et al., 2005.

claim: Ptpmt1 dephosphorylates phosphatidylinositol phosphates (PIPs).
source: It dephosphorylates phosphatidylinositol phosphates (PIPs).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is supported by citations in the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: PIPs bind to a distinctive set of effector proteins, thereby regulating cellular processes including membrane trafficking and ion channel/transporter functions.
source: PIPs are a class of membrane phospholipids that bind to a distinctive set of effector proteins, thereby regulating a characteristic suite of cellular processes, including membrane trafficking and ion channel/transporter functions (Balla, 2006; Gamper and Shapiro, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balla, 2006 and Gamper and Shapiro, 2007.

claim: Ptpmt1 is involved in the synthesis of cardiolipin by converting phosphotidylglecerol phosphate to phosphotidylglecerol, the precursor of cardiolipin.
source: Ptpmt1 is also involved in the synthesis of cardiolipin by converting phosphotidylglecerol phosphate to phosphotidylglecerol, the precursor of cardiolipin (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: Global knockout of Ptpmt1 results in developmental arrest and post-implantation lethality.
source: Global knockout of Ptpmt1 results in developmental arrest and post-implantation lethality (Zhang et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2011 and Shen et al., 2011.

claim: Ptpmt1 facilitates mitochondrial metabolism largely by dephosphorylation of downstream PIP substrates.
source: Our previous studies suggest that Ptpmt1 facilitates mitochondrial metabolism largely by dephosphorylation of downstream PIP substrates (Yu et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors (Yu et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2009).

claim: PIP substrates appear to inhibit mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation but enhance cytosolic glycolysis by activation of mitochondrial uncoupling protein 2 (Ucp2).
source: that appear to inhibit mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation but enhance cytosolic glycolysis by activation of mitochondrial uncoupling protein 2 (Ucp2) (Yu et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Ucp2 is a transporter of four-carbon (C4) dicarboxylate intermediates of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle.
source: a transporter of four-carbon (C4) dicarboxylate intermediates of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle that has been shown to regulate cellular energetics by limiting mitochondrial oxidation of glucose (Vozza et al., 2014; Bouillaud, 2009; Diano and Horvath, 2012; Pecqueur et al., 2008; Samudio et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vozza et al., 2014; Bouillaud, 2009; Diano and Horvath, 2012; Pecqueur et al., 2008; Samudio et al., 2009.

claim: Ucp2 regulates cellular energetics by limiting mitochondrial oxidation of glucose.
source: that has been shown to regulate cellular energetics by limiting mitochondrial oxidation of glucose (Vozza et al., 2014; Bouillaud, 2009; Diano and Horvath, 2012; Pecqueur et al., 2008; Samudio et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vozza et al., 2014; Bouillaud, 2009; Diano and Horvath, 2012; Pecqueur et al., 2008; Samudio et al., 2009.

claim: Ptpmt1 is highly expressed in the heart and skeletal muscle.
source: Ptpmt1 is highly expressed in the heart and skeletal muscle (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2011.

claim: Ptpmt1 was ~95% deleted in skeletal muscle of Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription PCR showed ~95% and ~80% deletion of Ptpmt1 in the skeletal muscle and heart in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative reverse transcription PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ptpmt1 was ~80% deleted in heart of Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription PCR showed ~95% and ~80% deletion of Ptpmt1 in the skeletal muscle and heart in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative reverse transcription PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice were indistinguishable from their wild-type littermates up to 3 months of age.
source: These animals were indistinguishable from their wild-type (WT, Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+) littermates up to 3 months of age, suggesting that Ptpmt1 deletion did not affect muscle or heart development.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Ptpmt1 deletion did not affect muscle or heart development.
source: These animals were indistinguishable from their wild-type (WT, Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+) littermates up to 3 months of age, suggesting that Ptpmt1 deletion did not affect muscle or heart development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that knockout mice were indistinguishable from wild-type up to 3 months.

claim: Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ knockout mice exhibited reduced weight gain starting at 4–5 months.
source: The knockout mice exhibited reduced weight gain starting at 4–5 months and their body sizes were significantly smaller than those of control mice at 8 months (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data and Figure 1A.

claim: Body sizes of Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice were significantly smaller than those of control mice at 8 months.
source: The knockout mice exhibited reduced weight gain starting at 4–5 months and their body sizes were significantly smaller than those of control mice at 8 months (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data and Figure 1A.

claim: Muscle wasting was observed in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice at 8 months or older.
source: Muscle wasting was observed in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice at 8 months or older (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data and Figure 1A.

claim: Histopathological examination of skeletal muscles of Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice revealed marked variations in muscle fiber diameters and the presence of ghost fibers or more interstitial space.
source: Histopathological examination of skeletal muscles of these knockout mice revealed characteristic changes of muscle atrophy – marked variations in muscle fiber diameters and the presence of ghost fibers or more interstitial space (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological examination data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Masson's Trichrome staining revealed increased collagen-rich fibrotic regions in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles.
source: In addition, Masson's Trichrome staining revealed increased collagen-rich fibrotic regions in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Masson's Trichrome staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice became fatigued faster and fell more quickly than control animals in wire hang tests.
source: Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice became fatigued faster and fell more quickly than Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+ control animals in wire hang tests, indicating muscle weakness (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by wire hang test data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both male and female Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ knockout mice displayed reduced maximum speed in treadmill exercise tests.
source: In treadmill exercise tests, both male and female knockout mice displayed reduced maximum speed (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by treadmill exercise test data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both male and female Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ knockout mice displayed reduced endurance in treadmill exercise tests.
source: In treadmill exercise tests, both male and female knockout mice displayed reduced maximum speed (Figure 1D), endurance (Figure 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by treadmill exercise test data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both male and female Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ knockout mice displayed reduced distance of the run in treadmill exercise tests.
source: In treadmill exercise tests, both male and female knockout mice displayed reduced maximum speed (Figure 1D), endurance (Figure 1E), and distance of the run (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by treadmill exercise test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus and EDL showed decreased optimal length.
source: Both knockout Soleus and EDL showed decreased optimal length, the length of the muscle at which maximal force was achieved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo force–frequency measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Specific force production of Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus was decreased.
source: Specific force production of Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and EDL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) was decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo force measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Specific force production of Ptpmt1 knockout EDL was decreased.
source: Specific force production of Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and EDL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) was decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo force measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Normalized force production was decreased in Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus.
source: However, normalized force production was decreased only in knockout Soleus (Figure 1F), but not in knockout EDL (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo force measurement data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Normalized force production was not decreased in Ptpmt1 knockout EDL.
source: However, normalized force production was decreased only in knockout Soleus (Figure 1F), but not in knockout EDL (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo force measurement data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ptpmt1 plays a more important role in oxidative than glycolytic muscle fibers.
source: These data suggest that Ptpmt1 plays a more important role in oxidative than glycolytic muscle fibers although both knockout Soleus and EDL developed muscle atrophy subsequently.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects on normalized force production in Soleus versus EDL.

claim: Both Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus and EDL developed muscle atrophy.
source: These data suggest that Ptpmt1 plays a more important role in oxidative than glycolytic muscle fibers although both knockout Soleus and EDL developed muscle atrophy subsequently.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Plasma glucose levels were comparable in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ and Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+ mice.
source: To determine the impact of Ptpmt1 depletion from the skeletal muscle and heart on the metabolism of the whole body, we measured plasma glucose and fatty acid levels and found that they were comparable in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ and Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by plasma glucose measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Plasma fatty acid levels were comparable in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ and Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+ mice.
source: To determine the impact of Ptpmt1 depletion from the skeletal muscle and heart on the metabolism of the whole body, we measured plasma glucose and fatty acid levels and found that they were comparable in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ and Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by plasma fatty acid measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Plasma levels of lactate in Ptpmt1 knockout mice were relatively normal.
source: Plasma levels of lactate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and lipid metabolic products (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) in Ptpmt1 knockout mice were also relatively normal (except that cholesterol and nonesterified fatty acids levels were decreased and marginally increased, respectively, in female knockout mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by plasma lactate measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cholesterol levels were decreased in female Ptpmt1 knockout mice.
source: Plasma levels of lactate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and lipid metabolic products (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) in Ptpmt1 knockout mice were also relatively normal (except that cholesterol and nonesterified fatty acids levels were decreased and marginally increased, respectively, in female knockout mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by cholesterol measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Nonesterified fatty acids levels were marginally increased in female Ptpmt1 knockout mice.
source: Plasma levels of lactate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and lipid metabolic products (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) in Ptpmt1 knockout mice were also relatively normal (except that cholesterol and nonesterified fatty acids levels were decreased and marginally increased, respectively, in female knockout mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by nonesterified fatty acids measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Adipokine array assays of the plasma showed no or subtle differences in Adiponectin, Leptin, Lipocalin-2, Angptl3, Resistin, Fgf-21, Dppiv, Fetuin A, Igf-1, etc. between Ptpmt1 knockout and control mice.
source: Adipokine array assays of the plasma showed no or subtle differences in Adiponectin, Leptin, Lipocalin-2, Angptl3, Resistin, Fgf-21, Dppiv, Fetuin A, Igf-1, etc. between Ptpmt1 knockout and control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by adipokine array assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: No differences in glucose tolerance tests were observed between Ptpmt1 knockout and control mice.
source: In addition, no differences in glucose tolerance tests were observed between Ptpmt1 knockout and control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: No changes in Hk2, Pkm1, Ldha, Dicer1, Mcad (Acadm), Acadl, Hadha, Cpt2, or Fabp3 were found in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles.
source: Furthermore, we assessed the expression levels of key enzymes involved in glucose and lipid metabolism in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles. No changes in Hk2, Pkm1, Ldha, Dicer1, Mcad (Acadm), Acadl, Hadha, Cpt2, or Fabp3 were found.
evidence: The claim is based on expression level assessment data.

claim: The expression of Cpt1B was increased in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles.
source: However, the expression of Cpt1B was increased in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression level data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G.

claim: Systemic glucose and lipid metabolism in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice was not significantly changed.
source: These results suggest that systemic glucose and lipid metabolism in these tissue-specific knockout mice was not significantly changed, but fatty acid partitioning for oxidation in the mitochondria was elevated in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the various metabolic measurements showing no significant changes.

claim: Fatty acid partitioning for oxidation in the mitochondria was elevated in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles.
source: These results suggest that systemic glucose and lipid metabolism in these tissue-specific knockout mice was not significantly changed, but fatty acid partitioning for oxidation in the mitochondria was elevated in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased expression of Cpt1B and other metabolic data.

claim: Ragged red fibers were observed in Ptpmt1 knockout skeletal muscles.
source: Gömöri trichrome staining revealed ragged red fibers in Ptpmt1 knockout skeletal muscles (Figure 2A), as observed in various types of human mitochondrial myopathies.
evidence: The claim is supported by Gömöri trichrome staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Interfibrillar mitochondria in knockout Soleus and EDL were disorganized and enlarged.
source: Electron microscopic analyses showed that interfibrillar mitochondria in knockout Soleus and EDL were disorganized and enlarged, in contrast to normal mitochondria that typically reside in pairs and position on either side of the Z-disc in control muscles.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopic analysis data.

claim: There was a massive accumulation of subsarcolemmal mitochondria in the knockout muscles.
source: In addition, there was a massive accumulation of subsarcolemmal mitochondria in the knockout muscles, whereas the content of intermyofibrillar mitochondria decreased (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopic analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The content of intermyofibrillar mitochondria decreased in the knockout muscles.
source: In addition, there was a massive accumulation of subsarcolemmal mitochondria in the knockout muscles, whereas the content of intermyofibrillar mitochondria decreased (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopic analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mitochondrial structural changes appeared to be more severe in EDL than Soleus in the knockout mice.
source: Although EDL, unlike Soleus, uses more cytosolic glycolysis than mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation for energy production, the mitochondrial structural changes appeared to be more severe in EDL than Soleus in the knockout mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopic analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A massive accumulation of intramyofibrillar lipids were detected in 6 months or older Ptpmt1 knockout muscles.
source: Furthermore, a massive accumulation of intramyofibrillar lipids were detected by Oil Red O staining in 6 months or older Ptpmt1 knockout muscles (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Total mitochondrial content in Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus and EDL slightly decreased compared to that in control muscles.
source: Total mitochondrial content in Ptpmt1 knockout Soleus and EDL also slightly decreased compared to that in control muscles (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial content measurement data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ATP levels in both knockout Soleus and EDL decreased significantly compared to WT counterparts.
source: ATP levels in both knockout Soleus and EDL decreased significantly compared to WT counterparts (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP level measurement data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: AMP-activated kinase (Ampk) was highly activated in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ muscles.
source: Consistent with these data, the energetic stress sensor, AMP-activated kinase (Ampk), was highly activated in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ muscles as determined by the phosphorylation levels of Thr172 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acc) was inhibited in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ muscles.
source: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acc), a negative regulator of fatty acid oxidation, was inhibited, as evidenced by a marked increase in the inhibitory phosphorylation of this enzyme (Figure 2F), implying increased fatty acid oxidation in Ptpmt1-depleted mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Increased fatty acid oxidation is implied in Ptpmt1-depleted mitochondria.
source: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acc), a negative regulator of fatty acid oxidation, was inhibited, as evidenced by a marked increase in the inhibitory phosphorylation of this enzyme (Figure 2F), implying increased fatty acid oxidation in Ptpmt1-depleted mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the inhibition of Acc, a negative regulator of fatty acid oxidation.

claim: Ampk negatively regulates mTor signaling.
source: In agreement with previous findings that Ampk negatively regulates mTor signaling (Hardie, 2015; Liang and Mills, 2013), mTor was substantially inhibited.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hardie, 2015 and Liang and Mills, 2013.

claim: mTor was substantially inhibited in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ muscles.
source: In agreement with previous findings that Ampk negatively regulates mTor signaling (Hardie, 2015; Liang and Mills, 2013), mTor was substantially inhibited.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Activities of S6k, S6, and 4E-bp1 were concomitantly decreased in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ muscles.
source: Activities of S6k, S6, and 4E-bp1, key downstream components of mTor signaling, were also concomitantly decreased (Figure 2F), indicating diminished anabolic activities and consistent with the muscle atrophy phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Akt activities were increased in Ptpmt1 knockout skeletal muscles.
source: Interestingly, Akt activities, as reflected by its phosphorylation levels (Ser473 and Thr308), were increased in Ptpmt1 knockout skeletal muscles, recapitulating mTor and raptor (a component of the mTor complex 1) knockout muscles (Bentzinger et al., 2008; Risson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F and citations to Bentzinger et al., 2008 and Risson et al., 2009.

claim: Erk activities were slightly increased in Ptpmt1 knockout skeletal muscles.
source: Likely due to the cross-talk between Akt and Ras signaling pathways, Erk activities were also slightly increased in these knockout muscles (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F and inferred from cross-talk between signaling pathways.

claim: Expression levels of electron transport chain complexes in Ptpmt1-ablated mitochondria were not changed in young knockout mice.
source: Expression levels of electron transport chain complexes in these Ptpmt1-ablated mitochondria were not changed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Total cellular ATP levels in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles at 3 months were comparable to those in control tissues.
source: Total cellular ATP levels in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles at this age were comparable to those in control tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP level measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ptpmt1 knockout muscles at 3 months did not show bioenergetic/metabolic stress.
source: and the knockout muscles did not show bioenergetic/metabolic stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No evidence of elevated autophagic activities was found in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles at 3 months.
source: We also checked Lc3-I/II levels in Ptpmt1 knockout muscles and found no evidence of elevated autophagic activities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The decrease in total cellular ATP levels in older knockout muscles was a secondary not direct effect of Ptpmt1 depletion.
source: These results indicate that the decrease in total cellular ATP levels in older knockout muscles (Figure 2E) was a secondary not direct effect of Ptpmt1 depletion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that young knockout muscles had normal ATP levels.

claim: Knockout muscle tissues showed decreased maximal reserve oxidative capacities in the presence of full metabolic substrates.
source: Knockout muscle tissues showed decreased maximal reserve oxidative capacities in the presence of full metabolic substrates (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption rate measurement data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATP synthesis-driven oxygen consumption in Ptpmt1-deficient mitochondria was markedly decreased when pyruvate was provided as the sole substrate.
source: When pyruvate, a critical metabolite derived from glucose, was provided as the sole substrate, ATP synthesis-driven oxygen consumption in Ptpmt1-deficient mitochondria was markedly decreased (Figure 3B), suggesting that mitochondrial utilization of pyruvate was diminished in the absence of Ptpmt1.
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption measurement data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mitochondrial utilization of pyruvate was diminished in the absence of Ptpmt1.
source: When pyruvate, a critical metabolite derived from glucose, was provided as the sole substrate, ATP synthesis-driven oxygen consumption in Ptpmt1-deficient mitochondria was markedly decreased (Figure 3B), suggesting that mitochondrial utilization of pyruvate was diminished in the absence of Ptpmt1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the decreased oxygen consumption with pyruvate as substrate.

claim: Enhanced oxygen consumption was observed in Ptpmt1-deficient mitochondria when fatty acids were supplied as the fuel.
source: Interestingly, we observed enhanced oxygen consumption in these mitochondria when fatty acids were supplied as the fuel (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption measurement data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A slightly increased respiratory response in Ptpmt1-depleted mitochondria was detected when glutamate was provided.
source: A slightly increased respiratory response in Ptpmt1-depleted mitochondria was also detected when glutamate, another mitochondrial substrate, was provided (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption measurement data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Feeding with succinate resulted in similar oxygen consumption in Ptpmt1 null and control mitochondria.
source: Importantly, feeding with succinate, the substrate for Complex II of the electron transport chain, resulted in similar oxygen consumption in Ptpmt1 null and control mitochondria (Figure 3E), validating the intact function of the electron transport chain in the knockout mitochondria and excluding flavin adenine dinucleotide and quinone-linked deficiencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption measurement data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The electron transport chain in the knockout mitochondria has intact function.
source: Importantly, feeding with succinate, the substrate for Complex II of the electron transport chain, resulted in similar oxygen consumption in Ptpmt1 null and control mitochondria (Figure 3E), validating the intact function of the electron transport chain in the knockout mitochondria and excluding flavin adenine dinucleotide and quinone-linked deficiencies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar oxygen consumption with succinate as substrate.

claim: Ptpmt1 plays an important role in facilitating carbohydrate oxidation in mitochondria.
source: These mechanistic data suggest that Ptpmt1 plays an important role in facilitating carbohydrate oxidation in mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the various metabolic data showing decreased pyruvate utilization in Ptpmt1-deficient mitochondria.

claim: Intramitochondrial pyruvate levels in the mitochondria freshly isolated from Ptpmt1 knockout muscles decreased by half.
source: Consistent with the above notion, intramitochondrial pyruvate levels in the mitochondria freshly isolated from Ptpmt1 knockout muscles decreased by half (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pyruvate level measurement data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Levels of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) decreased in the knockout mitochondria.
source: Levels of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), an important metabolite in the TCA cycle, also decreased in the knockout mitochondria (Figure 3G)
evidence: The claim is supported by α-KG level measurement data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Steady-state mitochondrial acetyl-CoA levels were not changed in Ptpmt1 knockout mitochondria.
source: although steady-state mitochondrial acetyl-CoA levels were not changed (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by acetyl-CoA level measurement data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: α-KG production in Ptpmt1-deficient mitochondria was decreased compared to that in control mitochondria.
source: To further determine if pyruvate transport efficiency may be reduced in Ptpmt1-ablated mitochondria, we incubated fresh mitochondria with pyruvate and measured acute production of α-KG from extramitochondrial pyruvate. As shown in Figure 3I, α-KG production in Ptpmt1-deficient mitochondria was indeed decreased compared to that in control mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by α-KG production measurement data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (Pdh) was not affected in the knockout mitochondria.
source: Notably, the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (Pdh), the enzyme that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA to feed the TCA cycle, was not affected in the knockout mitochondria (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pdh activity measurement data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Ptpmt1 null mitochondria were impaired in uptaking pyruvate.
source: These observations together with that the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier/transporter (Mpc) was comparably expressed in Ptpmt1-ablated mitochondria (Figure 2F) suggest that Ptpmt1 null mitochondria were impaired in uptaking pyruvate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from decreased intramitochondrial pyruvate levels, decreased α-KG production, and normal Pdh activity.

claim: Muscle fibers in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice switched from oxidative to glycolytic fibers.
source: Possibly due to an adaptive response to the inhibition of pyruvate oxidation in the mitochondria, skeletal muscle fiber-type switching occurred in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice. Muscle fibers in these knockout mice switched from oxidative to glycolytic fibers, as evidenced by a dramatic increase (~170-fold) in the levels of Myh4, a marker of glycolytic fast-twitch Type 2B fibers in Ptpmt1 knockout mice (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by Myh4 expression level data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: There was a dramatic increase (~170-fold) in the levels of Myh4 in Ptpmt1 knockout mice.
source: Muscle fibers in these knockout mice switched from oxidative to glycolytic fibers, as evidenced by a dramatic increase (~170-fold) in the levels of Myh4, a marker of glycolytic fast-twitch Type 2B fibers in Ptpmt1 knockout mice (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by Myh4 expression level data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The heart in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice was less impacted than the skeletal muscle.
source: The heart in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice was less impacted than the skeletal muscle although Ptpmt1 was ~80% deleted from the heart (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative observations of skeletal muscle and heart phenotypes.

claim: At 7 months, no evident histological changes were observed in heart tissues of Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice.
source: At 7 months, when skeletal muscles in these mice displayed atrophy and myocyte damage, no evident histological changes were observed in heart tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Echocardiographic examination showed no difference in left ventricle (LV) contractility in Ptpmt1 knockout mice at 7 months.
source: Echocardiographic examination showed no difference in left ventricle (LV) contractility in Ptpmt1 knockout mice as reflected by similar LV fractional shortening (FS), ejection fraction (EF), and the ratio of peak velocity of early to late filling of mitral inflow (E/A) between knockout and control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mitochondrial content in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ heart tissues was comparable to that in control tissues at 7 months.
source: Mitochondrial content in Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ heart tissues was comparable to that in Ptpmt1+/+/Ckm-Cre+ control tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial content measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Total ATP levels in Ptpmt1 knockout heart tissues were marginally but not significantly decreased at 7 months.
source: Total ATP levels in Ptpmt1 knockout heart tissues were marginally but not significantly decreased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP level measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mitochondria in knockout cardiomyocytes showed minimal structural changes at 7 months.
source: Moreover, mitochondria in knockout cardiomyocytes showed minimal structural changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopic examination data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No bioenergetic/metabolic stress was detected in the knockout cardiomyocytes at 7 months.
source: Consistent with these observations, no bioenergetic/metabolic stress was detected in the knockout cardiomyocytes according to the activation status of Ampk and mTor signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Severe cardiac dysfunction was observed in 10- to 12-month-old Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice.
source: However, severe cardiac dysfunction was observed in 10- to 12-month-old Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Cardiomyocytes in 10- to 12-month-old Ptpmt1fl/fl/Ckm-Cre+ mice had uneven sizes and were disorganized.

evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Skeletal muscle mitochondria prefer glucose as the substrate.
source: Mitochondria in the skeletal muscle and heart have distinct preferences for energy sources – skeletal muscle mitochondria prefer glucose (the major simple carbohydrate) as the substrate, whereas cardiac mitochondria mainly use fatty acids as the fuel.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Cardiac mitochondria mainly use fatty acids as the fuel.
source: Mitochondria in the skeletal muscle and heart have distinct preferences for energy sources – skeletal muscle mitochondria prefer glucose (the major simple carbohydrate) as the substrate, whereas cardiac mitochondria mainly use fatty acids as the fuel.

claim: In slow-twitch oxidative muscle fibers glucose (via pyruvate) is predominantly oxidized within the mitochondria to generate energy.
source: Moreover, different types of skeletal muscle cells (fibers) utilize glucose to produce energy in different mechanisms – in slow-twitch oxidative muscle fibers glucose (via pyruvate, a critical metabolite derived from glucose) is predominantly oxidized within the mitochondria to generate energy
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claim: In fast-twitch muscle fibers pyruvate is primarily reduced to lactate in the cytosol promoting glycolytic flux to rapidly produce energy and support quick contractions.

claim: Both muscle and heart mitochondria are flexible in selecting substrates in response to stress and under disease conditions.
source: Nevertheless, both muscle and heart mitochondria are flexible in selecting substrates in response to stress (exercise, fasting, etc.) and under disease conditions (heart failure, diabetes, etc.) (Bertero and Maack, 2018; Brown et al., 2017; Nabben et al., 2018; Schulze et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bertero and Maack, 2018; Brown et al., 2017; Nabben et al., 2018; Schulze et al., 2016.

claim: It remains to be determined how mitochondrial utilization of various competing metabolic substrates is coordinated.
